science.title: Assessment of interkingdom TIR domain interactions using a modular yeast tripartite split-GFP system
science.description: Thanks to its genetic resourcefulness, Saccharomyces cerevisiae has been traditionally used as a model organism to detect and study protein-protein interactions. The recent development of synthetic biology toolkits brings an opportunity to expand such utilities. Here, we coupled the modular cloning (MoClo) system to the tripartite split-GFP strategy to systematically study protein interactions in particular cellular localizations. To provide proof-of-principle of this yeast-based tripartite split-GFP (ytpGFP), we challenged interactions of bacterial TIR domain-containing proteins (Brucella BtpA and BtpB) between themselves, as well as against human TIR adaptors of the myddosome and triffosome innate immune signaling complexes. While fluorescence microscopy provided clues about which member of the interacting pair drives subcellular localization of the complex, interactions could be readily tracked and quantified by flow cytometry. The ytpGFP system detected known homotypic or heterotypic complexes and defined previously unknown interkingdom TIR-TIR interactions. Human MyD88, TIRAP, TRAM, and TRIF were capable of interacting with both BtpA and BtpB TIR domains with differing efficiency. Furthermore, our results suggest that the N-terminal non-TIR extensions of both BtpA and, especially, BtpB limit the ability of their TIR domains to interact. This strategy is a useful addition to other yeast-based tools to study protein complexes.

science.title: Membrane-coupled conformational switching of VISTA regulates CC′ loop accessibility and immune checkpoint signaling
science.description: V-domain immunoglobulin suppressor of T-cell activation (VISTA) is an immune checkpoint that suppresses T-cell responses and has emerged as a promising target for cancer immunotherapy. Here we show, using atomistic molecular dynamics simulations of both truncated glycan-free and full-length glycosylated membrane-bound human VISTA, that the extracellular and transmembrane domains remain structurally stable, while the unusually long CC′ loop is stabilized by extensive hydrogen-bonding interactions. Principal component analysis and conformational clustering reveal a recurrent rotational motion of the extracellular domain relative to the membrane, producing two conformational states: an “Up” state with a solvent-exposed CC′ loop and a “Down” state in which the loop transiently associates with the membrane. These transitions are coupled to proline-mediated bending of the transmembrane helix. We propose that this membrane-coupled Up/Down switching regulates CC′ loop accessibility, providing a structural mechanism that may influence VISTA-mediated immune checkpoint signaling.

science.title: Earth's fiery birth may have created hundreds of oceans' worth of water
science.description: Earth's water may have been born in the planet's fiery atmosphere rather than delivered by icy comets or asteroids. Scientists discovered that rocky pebbles reacting with hydrogen under extreme heat can produce water in minutes, potentially generating hundreds of oceans' worth during Earth's formation. The findings suggest that water may be a natural part of how rocky planets form, rather than something that must arrive from space.

science.title: SIP-enabled multi-omics reveals soil microbiome responses to drought and rehydration
science.description: Soil microbial activity, and the balance of anabolic (carbon assimilating) and catabolic (CO2-releasing) processes, control the magnitude and direction of soil carbon fluxes. Soil hydration controls this activity, and with hydroclimate volatility increasing across many regions, microbial responses to drought-rewetting cycles urgently require quantification. We conducted rainfall exclusion experiments at two Mediterranean-type field sites, coupling isotope labeling with multi-omics, to link microbial growth, greenhouse gas fluxes, and the carbon sources driving both. Rehydration shortened apparent cell generation times from years to days within minutes. High-intensity drought lengthened the lag before growth resumed, yet metagenomic inference indicated post-drought enrichment of rapid-growth phenotypes. Drought and rehydration shifted the soil metabolome, implicating specific osmolytes in the microbial response and suggesting metabolite diversity modulates microbial function. These results constrain soil microbial activity rates and mechanisms underlying drought-rewetting responses and motivate further study of carbon cycling under increasingly volatile hydroclimates. This study demonstrates that soil microbial growth rates are extremely slow under dry conditions, with rehydration causing a rapid increase in anabolic activity within days. These findings refine our understanding of microbial contributions to soil carbon cycling with a warming climate.
